# 1. Introduction

The reporting of standardized effect sizes has become a
near-universal expectation in the behavioral sciences, codified in
the *Publication Manual of the American Psychological Association*
[@apa2020] and embedded in editorial policy across psychology,
education, and the broader social sciences [@wilkinson1999;
@cumming2014]. Effect sizes quantify the magnitude of a phenomenon
on a metric that is comparable across studies, feed power analysis
and study planning, and supply the raw material for meta-analytic
synthesis. Effect-size reporting has accordingly been central to the
"new statistics" reform movement [@cumming2014], and recent
editorial mandates go beyond reporting to require interval estimates
and substantive interpretation [@apa2020].

Yet a foundational psychometric problem has remained largely
peripheral to this reform: standardized effect sizes computed from
fallible measures are systematically attenuated relative to the
population effect on the construct of interest. This attenuation,
formalized by @spearman1904, follows directly from classical test
theory: when an observed score $X$ is the sum of a true score $T$
and an independent random error $E$, the variance of $X$ exceeds
the variance of $T$, and any standardized contrast on $X$ is shrunk
toward zero. For the standardized mean difference, the relationship
takes the form

$$d_{\text{observed}} = d_{\text{true}} \cdot \sqrt{\rho_{xx}}$$

where $\rho_{xx}$ is the reliability of the dependent variable. The
same logic applies to correlation coefficients, where error in both
variables compounds the shrinkage [@spearman1904].

The practical consequences of this attenuation are not subtle.
@schmidt1996 traced the implications of ignoring measurement error
across 26 research scenarios spanning personnel selection,
educational evaluation, and clinical assessment, finding that
uncorrected effect estimates produced systematically misleading
substantive conclusions. @hunter2004 made the disattenuation logic
the foundation of an entire approach to meta-analysis, sometimes
termed "psychometric meta-analysis," in which observed effect sizes
are corrected for sampling error, range restriction, and unreliability
before synthesis. @baugh2002 argued that the routine reporting of
effect sizes corrected for score reliability should become standard
practice in educational and psychological measurement, and the
present paper takes that argument as its starting point.

## 1.1 The gap between methodological consensus and software support

The methodological case for measurement-corrected effect sizes is
neither novel nor contested. Spearman's correction has been a
textbook procedure for over a century, and Hunter and Schmidt's
psychometric meta-analysis framework has accumulated thousands of
applications in industrial-organizational psychology, education, and
related fields. What has not kept pace with the methodological
consensus is the routine availability of corrected estimates in
applied work. Two observations support this characterization.

First, the dominant general-purpose effect-size packages in the R
ecosystem do not implement reliability correction by default.
The widely used `effectsize` package [@bensh2020] computes Cohen's
*d*, Hedges' *g*, and many other indices, but
does not offer measurement-error correction as part of its core
functionality. Specialized packages cover narrow components of the
problem: `MBESS` [@kelley2007] provides confidence intervals for
several effect sizes, `psych` [@revelle2024] computes reliability
coefficients including coefficient $\omega$, and `metafor`
[@viechtbauer2010] performs meta-analytic synthesis. The closest
relative is `psychmeta` [@dahlke2019], which implements
Hunter--Schmidt artifact corrections, including unreliability
corrections for *d* via `correct_d()`, as part of its psychometric
meta-analysis machinery. `psychmeta` is oriented toward
meta-analytic databases: `correct_d()` takes previously computed
*d* values, obtains the correction by converting through the
point-biserial correlation, and does not offer the
heteroscedasticity-robust or bootstrap intervals evaluated here.
No package serves the single-study workflow of computing a
corrected *d*-family estimate from raw data, a formula, or summary
statistics together with interval estimation and meta-analytic
export.

Second, the routine application of corrections requires choices that
applied researchers cannot easily make without software guidance.
The classical Spearman correction yields a point estimate but does
not by itself provide an interval estimate; the standard
Hunter--Schmidt confidence interval [@hunter2004] treats
reliability as known and can undercover when reliability is poorly
estimated [@charles2005]; the Bonett *t*-distribution
refinement [@bonett2008] and bootstrap procedures
[see also @algina2003] offer alternatives, but their relative
performance under realistic conditions has not been systematically
mapped. As a consequence, the small minority of applied researchers
who apply disattenuation often do so without an interval estimate,
which limits the inferential value of the correction.


## 1.2 The present contribution

We address this gap by introducing the measuredES R package, which
implements measurement-corrected effect sizes under classical test
theory. The package provides corrected versions of Cohen's *d*,
Hedges' *g*, and Pearson correlations (the latter with a Fisher-z
interval), three confidence-interval methods for the *d* family
(Hunter--Schmidt analytical, Bonett, and BCa bootstrap), optional
propagation of reliability-estimation uncertainty through the
`rxx_se` argument, an APA-7 reporting interface, and a
meta-analytic export that feeds `metafor` directly. The
implementation favors single-function workflows, accepts summary
statistics as well as raw data, and ships with a vignette and a
reproducible test suite.

To evaluate both the package and the broader correction approach, we
conducted three connected Monte Carlo simulation studies and five
focused sub-studies, presented in this article. **Study 1** examined the bias and root-mean-square
error of corrected and uncorrected Cohen's *d* across a 192-cell
factorial design crossing true effect size, sample size, true
reliability, reliability estimation status (known versus estimated
via coefficient $\alpha$), and distributional form (normal versus
moderately skewed). **Study 2** evaluated the coverage probability
and width of the two analytical confidence-interval procedures
(Hunter--Schmidt and Bonett) across the same design factors; the
BCa bootstrap, too costly for the full factorial, was evaluated in
a focused sub-study (Section 5.2.4). **Study 3** moved the
analysis to the meta-analytic level,
examining the bias of pooled effect estimates under homogeneous
versus heterogeneous between-study reliability, with the number of
synthesized studies $k \in \{5, 10, 20\}$. The sub-studies
(Sections 4.5--4.6) probed the BCa bootstrap, severe skewness, the
propagation of reliability-estimation uncertainty, unbalanced and
heteroscedastic designs including the combined Behrens--Fisher
case, and the two-sided correction for correlations.

The remainder of this article is organized as follows. Section 2
develops the theoretical foundation: Spearman's correction and the
confidence-interval methods built on it. Section 3 introduces the
`measuredES` package. Section 4 describes the simulation design,
and Section 5 reports the results of the three studies. Section 6
discusses implications, practical recommendations, and limitations,
and Section 7 concludes.
